edition: Issue 021 - A new mum who out-ran an Olympian, a two billion dollar industry told to eat sunshine, and an MP who swore allegiance with her fingers crossed
tagline: Your 3-minute break. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: Camille French won the Melbourne marathon 11 months after her second baby - take that, timeline
stories.summary: Two-time Olympian Camille French, 36, won the women's Melbourne Marathon 11 months after having her second child, holding off Australian Olympian Sinead Diver.

body.text: New Zealander Camille French won the women's Melbourne Marathon on Sunday, finishing in 2 hours 28 minutes 25 seconds, just 11 months after giving birth to her second child. The 36-year-old, who ran for New Zealand in the 5000m and 10,000m at the 2017 world championships, the 2018 Commonwealth Games and the Tokyo Olympics, broke away from Australia's Sinead Diver after the 25km mark and held on by 24 seconds. It was only her fourth marathon. Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge won the men's race in a course record the same morning.

There is a particular brand of smugness reserved for people who come back from something, and nobody does it with more style than a 36-year-old mum casually running down an Olympic medallist less than a year after a baby. Every parent knows the real achievement: she found 42 uninterrupted kilometres. The sports-science books say you need a full year to rebuild after childbirth, and Camille French looked at that timeline, yawned, and ran through it at 2:28 pace.

Scoop (Athletics NZ, 11 Oct 2026): Camille French won the women's Melbourne Marathon in 2:28:25, 24 seconds ahead of Australia's Sinead Diver (2:28:49), with Ireland's Nichola Sheridan third. French ran for NZ at the 2017 world championships, 2018 Commonwealth Games and Tokyo Olympics, and ran a 2:26:08 women's marathon debut in Valencia in Dec 2023. ABC News (11 Oct 2026) confirmed the result and noted Eliud Kipchoge broke the men's course record.

stories.headline: The Government rejected tariff protection for the two billion dollar NZ aluminium industry. The EU protects its own at 50 percent.
stories.summary: Commerce Minister Cameron Brewer declined the aluminium extrusion industry's bid for safeguard tariffs on a flood of Chinese imports, a decision the industry calls a death warrant for plants and more than 1000 jobs.

body.text: The Government has declined to give New Zealand's aluminium extrusion industry temporary protection against a surge of cheap imports. The industry, which makes the aluminium that ends up in window and door frames, trucks, boats and building components, had asked for a safeguard measure, a short-term quota or tariff. Commerce Minister Cameron Brewer declined the application after an MBIE report found the strict threshold had not been met, despite acknowledging serious injury. The industry body says the refusal puts more than 1,000 skilled manufacturing jobs at risk.

There is something deeply Kiwi about being the only comparable aluminium-producing country on Earth that decides not to use the trade tools everyone else uses. The EU slaps a 50 percent safeguard duty on the same Chinese aluminium, the US keeps tariffs of similar magnitude, and Australia, Canada, the UK and Brazil all have measures, while New Zealand decided its industry should compete against imports priced below the cost of the raw metal. It is a noble, principled position, the kind where you wave goodbye to a thousand skilled jobs and say, well, at least we were well-mannered about it.

RNZ (13 Oct 2026, business): Commerce Minister Cameron Brewer declined a request by the Aluminium Extruders Association for a safeguard measure after an MBIE report found the legal threshold was not met despite acknowledging serious injury. The Post (13 Oct 2026) reported import volumes of aluminium extrusions spiked 33 percent in the first three months of 2026, and quoted industry chair Nick Collins saying the EU applies a 50 percent safeguard duty and the US tariffs of similar magnitude while New Zealand applies none. E tu said more than 1,000 manufacturing jobs across Hamilton, New Plymouth and Wellington were at risk.

stories.headline: A new Scottish MP has to swear loyalty to the King. So she crossed her fingers.
stories.summary: New SNP MP Lara Bird crossed her fingers while taking the oath of allegiance to King Charles III required to take her Westminster seat, a gesture she confirmed was intentional to signal her first loyalty is to her constituents.

body.text: New Scottish National Party MP Lara Bird crossed her fingers while taking the oath of allegiance to King Charles III that is legally required to sit in the UK Parliament. Bird, who won the Arbroath and Broughty Ferry by-election, began her swearing-in by saying she took the oath only so she could serve her constituents, and that her primary loyalty would always be to the sovereign people of Scotland. She told The Courier her action was intentional, that she was not the first Nationalist MP to do it and would not be the last.

There is a schoolyard elegance to this that we should all respect. You are legally required to promise loyalty to a crown you do not support, and you are not allowed into the room otherwise, so you do the absolute minimum, and cross your fingers like a ten-year-old promising your flatmate you will definitely do the dishes. It is principled defiance delivered with the energy of a playground loophole. The really funny bit is the Westminster establishment being scandalised that an MP would prefer her own constituents to a hereditary monarch.

The Courier (2026): new SNP MP Lara Bird confirmed she intentionally crossed her fingers while taking the oath of allegiance to King Charles III, a legal requirement to take her Westminster seat after winning the Arbroath and Broughty Ferry by-election, and said she would not be the last to do so. The National and LBC reported backlash from conservative commentators after she posted video of the swearing-in, and that former MP Steven Bonnar did the same in 2019. The Scotsman reported Stephen Gethins defended her as an upgrade for the seat. MPs who decline the oath are barred from sitting in the Commons.

affiliate_cta.headline: Champion-level focus? Here is what we would look at.
affiliate_cta.body: Between a mum who ran down an Olympian, an industry fighting against the price of its own raw metal, and an MP running a protest through the constitution, this edition is a reminder that the small sensible choices are the ones that hold up. No pitch, no pressure: just a calm look before you commit to anything.
